t: Distinct Prime Factors of Product of Array — Factorize Each Element
o: Prime factors of a product are exactly the union of prime factors of the elements — never compute the astronomically large product. Just factorize each nums[i] (<= 1000) and collect distinct primes in a set. Example 1: union of factors of {2,4,3,7,10,6} = {2,3,5,7} → 4. Example 2: powers of 2 only → 1. With n up to 1e4 and values <= 1000, trial division per element is trivially fast; alternatively precompute smallest-prime-factor by sieve up to 1000.
k: Union of per-element prime factor sets equals the product's prime factor set.
Values <= 1000 mean at most 4 distinct primes per number (2·3·5·7=210, ·11 > 1000).
A sieve of smallest prime factors gives O(log v) factorization per element.

a.n: Approach 1: Per-Element Trial Division into a Set
a.i: For each number, strip factors d = 2, 3, 4, ... up to sqrt(v), inserting each distinct prime found into a hash set; insert the leftover if > 1. Return the set size.
s: For each v: for d in 2..sqrt(v), if d divides v add d and divide out all copies.
a.t: O(n·√V) — trial division per element with V <= 1000, so effectively O(n).
a.sp: O(π(V)) — the set of distinct primes (at most 168).

a.i: Precompute spf[v] for v <= 1000 once; then each element factorizes by repeated spf jumps in O(log v). Better asymptotics per element and cleaner logic; worthwhile if values were larger or queries many.
s: Factor each nums[i] via spf chain, adding primes to a set.
a.t: O(M log log M + n log V) — sieve plus logarithmic factorizations.

w: Never build the product — it has thousands of digits. Both approaches are fine here; prefer SPF sieve if the interviewer asks about scaling to larger values (then sieve up to max(nums)). Edge cases: single-element arrays, prime elements themselves, and duplicated primes across elements (set dedupes automatically).
